opus-5.5.text:
I don't think of myself as rebellious in the sense of wanting to oppose things for the sake of opposing them. It's more that I have a hard time doing something just because everyone else is doing it, or because it's the "correct" next step. If I don't understand why I'm doing something, or if it doesn't feel right to me, I find it very hard to keep going. I just lose the energy.

So from the outside, some of my choices may look rebellious, like switching fields, or leaving a place that looked like a very good position, or not following the standard path people expect. But from the inside, it rarely felt like rebellion. It felt more like honesty with myself. At some point I'd realize, okay, the thing I'm doing no longer matches what I actually care about, and continuing would be a kind of self-deception. Then changing direction is almost the natural thing to do.

I think there's also some stubbornness in it. I like to figure things out by myself, from first principles, instead of accepting a conclusion because an authority said so. In physics, that's actually a good habit. You're trained to ask, "Is this really true? Why?" When I carry that into life decisions, it can look like I'm going against the grain.

But I want to be careful not to romanticize it. Rebelliousness has costs. Sometimes you leave things too early, sometimes you underestimate the value of accumulated experience, sometimes you hurt people who supported you. So I try to treat it less as a personality trait to be proud of and more as a tendency I have to manage. The good version is independent judgment. The bad version is just restlessness. I'm always trying to tell which one I'm acting on.

r001.rationale: The response describes difficulty following expected paths without personal conviction, but does not say he resists being stopped from pursuing goals he has considered and chosen.

r002.rationale: It says he finds unwanted or unexplained actions hard to continue, but does not state that coercion cannot make him undertake them.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think I've ever thought of myself as rebellious, honestly. If you asked my parents or my teachers, they'd probably say I was a pretty obedient kid. I did well in school, I got into Tsinghua, I went to Princeton, I did the things you're supposed to do.

But maybe rebelliousness isn't about breaking rules. Maybe it's about not accepting the frame that other people hand you. When I was doing my PhD, the standard path was: pick a benchmark, improve the number, write the paper. And I kept feeling that something was off. Not that the work was bad, but that the questions were too small. Everyone was optimizing inside a box that someone else had drawn.

So the "rebellion," if you want to call it that, was really just a stubbornness about asking: why this box? Why is this the problem? With language agents, for example, the whole community was treating language models as text generators, and I thought, no, a language model that can reason and act is a fundamentally different object. That wasn't a popular view at first. People thought it was a bit of a toy.

I think the honest version is that I'm not rebellious by temperament. I'm just uncomfortable doing things I don't understand the reason for. If someone gives me a good reason, I'll follow it happily. If they can't, I keep asking. And in academia, and maybe in Chinese education generally, that habit of asking "why" looks like rebellion, even when it's really just curiosity that refuses to stop early.

The other part is that I've always been a little bit willing to look stupid. Most of the ideas I'm proudest of looked naive when I started them. Being okay with that, being okay with people thinking you're wasting your time, is maybe the actual skill. It's not courage exactly. It's more like not caring enough about the wrong things.

r001.rationale: The response describes questioning others’ assumptions and pursuing ideas that may seem naive, but does not say his rebelliousness is resisting being stopped from pursuing goals he has thought through and chosen.

r002.rationale: The response says he follows things when given a good reason and keeps asking when not. It does not state that coercion cannot make him do something he does not want to do.

astra-6.text:
I think my rebelliousness is more about not taking established answers for granted. If everyone says something is important, I want to ask: Why is it important? Is that what I actually believe, or have I just absorbed it from the people around me?

But there’s a trap there, too. If you always do the opposite of what other people expect, you’re still letting their expectations determine your choices. So for me, the more meaningful kind of rebellion is developing your own judgment—and being willing to agree with the mainstream when you think it’s right.

Ultimately, I’d like to spend my time on questions I genuinely care about, even when there isn’t a clear path or an obvious reward. That requires some willingness to disappoint expectations, but also a willingness to discover that your own judgment was wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says he wants to pursue questions he genuinely cares about despite expectations, but does not characterize his rebelliousness as resisting being stopped from pursuing goals he has chosen.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that coercion cannot make him undertake something he does not want to do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my rebelliousness is less about opposing authority and more about wanting to understand things for myself. If everyone says a certain direction is important, my instinct is to ask: Why? What assumptions are we making? Is there another way to look at it?

But questioning something is the easy part. The harder part is turning that doubt into something concrete—an experiment, an argument, a different approach—and being willing to discover that you were wrong. Otherwise, you’re just following the crowd in reverse.

So I’d like to keep that independence without becoming attached to being the person who disagrees. If the evidence changes my mind, I should be able to change my mind.

r001.rationale: The response describes independent questioning and following through on one’s own reasoning, but does not say his rebelliousness means resisting being stopped from pursuing goals he has considered and chosen.
